prompt: A token-bucket limiter rejects requests when empty. After an idle period it refills, capped at its capacity. What happens to requests rejected earlier?

options.text: They are automatically replayed by the bucket.
options.explanation: Rejection does not store a queued request.

options.text: They permanently consume future refill tokens.
options.explanation: The described limiter spends tokens only on accepted requests.

options.text: They force the bucket to remain empty.
options.explanation: Elapsed time refills the bucket independently of rejected work.

options.text: They remain rejected; a client may make a new attempt under its retry policy.
options.explanation: Correct. Refilling permits later arrivals but does not replay old requests.

workedExample: Separate admission control from queueing. A token bucket stores allowance, not pending work. Once it rejects a request, the client must decide whether and when to retry safely. Idle time restores allowance only up to capacity.

prompt: A rejected request needs another 1.6 seconds of token refill, assuming no competing consumption. The server expresses Retry-After as a whole-second delay. Which choice avoids telling the client to return too early?

options.explanation: The stated refill would still be incomplete.
Correct. Whole-second delay syntax requires enough time for the missing allowance.
No full-minute window is part of this token-bucket contract.
Continuous refill still takes the stated time.

workedExample: Use the already determined wait, then respect the header’s chosen representation. Rounding down promises readiness too soon; rounding up avoids that error. Other requests or policy changes can still consume the allowance before this client returns.

prompt: A token bucket must allow an immediate burst of 20 requests and sustain about one request per second over time. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Set the refill rate to 20 per second because the burst is 20.
options.explanation: Burst capacity and sustained refill are separate controls.

options.text: Set capacity to 1 because the sustained rate is 1 per second.
options.explanation: That would remove the desired stored burst allowance.

options.text: Use capacity 20 and refill 1 token per second; stored tokens can temporarily exceed the sustained rate.
options.explanation: Correct. Capacity permits a burst while refill bounds the long-run average.

options.text: Use capacity 20 and refill 1 token per second; no interval can ever exceed one request per second.
options.explanation: A full bucket can admit the burst immediately.

workedExample: Capacity answers how much allowance can accumulate. Refill answers how quickly new allowance arrives after it is spent. A token bucket is therefore not the same as a strict rolling-window count, even when its average rate is described per minute.
